jobs.title: We Never Handed the Whole Patient Conversation to One Model
jobs.description: Patient Conversations Were Never Handed to One Model Skip to content See the Benchmarks Behind Healthcare Call Center Performance Download the Report Topics: 01. Before the Models: Linguistics and a Knowledge Graph 02. The GPTeam Rule: Production or It Failed 03. Why We Wouldn't Ship It 04. Smaller Models We Can Explain 05. The Reality of a Health System 06. We Use the Big Models. We Don't Depend on Them. 07. Resolution Over Conversation Share this post When ChatGPT set off the generative-AI wave in early 2023, we saw the potential right away, and we knew better than to trust it too fast. So we pointed it at one of the hardest, most valuable problems we had: finding a patient an available appointment slot with the right provider, over the phone. The first time, it failed. The model spoke fluently and offered slots that didn’t exist, times that were never really on the calendar. We tried again as the models improved, and for a long stretch it still wasn’t reliable enough to put in front of a patient. Getting it right took three years and several generations of these models, and why we waited that long is the whole story of how we built it. Before the Models: Linguistics and a Knowledge Graph Long before any of this, we weren’t using language models at all. Back in 2019, the state of the art for our team was semantic parsing: a model that takes a sentence and breaks it into its parts, the nouns, the verbs, the adjectives. We had people with backgrounds in linguistics sitting next to the engineers. We’d take that parsed sentence and map it against a knowledge graph we built from a health system’s own data, starting with its website and provider directory. If a patient asked for Dr. Avery, someone who speaks Spanish, and we had both in the graph, we could connect them and return a list of doctors as cards. Those cards haven’t changed. What changed is everything behind them, how we understand what a patient wants. That is the pattern we’ve held for seven years: the patient still gets the same simple card, and we absorb all the complexity it takes to put the right answer on it. The GPTeam Rule: Production or It Failed When we got serious about language models, we put a team in a room and gave ourselves one rule: a project counts only if it reaches production. Anything that stays a prototype is a failure. Entity extraction—pulling dates, names, and other identifying details out of a sentence—passed that test almost immediately. Pulling a date of birth or a zip code out of a sentence replaced years of brittle code we’d maintained to handle every way a person might phrase the same thing. Scheduling did not pass. And the way it kept failing shaped everything that came after. Why We Wouldn't Ship It Negotiating a date and time sounds trivial until you do it in voice, where a patient can say “only Monday mornings, and not for two weeks.” The temptation, every single time, was to write one large prompt that handled the entire conversation. And every time we made that prompt bigger, we trusted it less. A larger context gives a model more room to contradict its own instructions, and far less room for us to explain what it did. Smaller Models We Can Explain So we went the other way. We broke scheduling into seven smaller jobs, each handled by its own focused model. One understands the date and time constraints a patient gives. Another’s only responsibility is to look at the genuinely available slots and offer a few. Another answers questions. Each one gets only the context it needs, nothing more. The result was fewer hallucinations and, just as importantly, a system we could debug. Here is what I mean. Say a patient books a primary care visit and mentions a mammogram in passing. In one big model, a stray detail like that can quietly steer the conversation, and afterward no one can tell you why. In ours, the step that answers questions does one narrow thing, so we can see exactly what it did with that detail and answer for it. When a health system asks why the agent said something on a specific call, “the model decided” is not an answer we’d ever give. We can show them exactly what happened. The Reality of a Health System Most of the industry treats the complexity of a health system as something to engineer around. We treat it as the reason we exist. Scheduling a single primary care appointment sounds simple until you account for provider availability across a multi-facility system, insurance rules, referral requirements, and real-time slot data pulled from the EHR. To get that right, the agent has to work from the same live systems your staff do, the medical record, the real scheduling data, the tools that actually run the operation, not a general guess about how healthcare usually works. This is where a general model, handed a prompt, gives you a smooth conversation and the wrong answer, because it is guessing. Our models are trained on the messy, specific ways real patients ask for care, the synonyms, the half-sentences, the constraints that only make sense inside one organization. That knowledge doesn’t live in a general training corpus. It lives in the interactions we’ve handled for years. We Use the Big Models. We Don't Depend on Them. We use OpenAI, Gemini, and others in our stack. We just don’t hand the stack to any of them. We build with fallback at every layer: if one vendor times out, we switch without the caller noticing, and if a region goes down, we route around it. The train doesn’t stop. We swap the engine while it’s moving. We do it that way because anything you rely on without a backup will fail you eventually. You just haven’t hit the day it does. But the deeper reason is the same one behind everything above. The moment a single model owns the whole conversation, you’ve given away the thing that matters most to us, which is knowing why it did what it did. Resolution Over Conversation Sounding human is easy now. Anyone can build a demo that holds a smooth conversation. A real resolution

jobs.title: 6 Health System Leaders Agree: Governance Is the Real Agentic AI Bottleneck
jobs.description: 6 Health System Leaders Agree: Governance Is the Real Agentic AI Bottleneck Skip to content See the Benchmarks Behind Healthcare Call Center Performance Download the Report Topics: 01. Face the governance sprawl head on 02. Earn trust in small workflows first 03. Standardize the workflow before you scale agentic AI 04. Don’t limit governance to standalone agentic AI projects 05. What separates the health systems getting this right 06. Scaling agentic AI means changing the workflow Share this post Key takeaways: Scaling agentic AI requires unified governance across IT, clinical, operational, legal, and executive teams. Trust is built through smaller, lower-risk workflows before AI agents move into higher-stakes use cases. AI agents expose inconsistent workflows, making standardization and change management critical to scaling. Many health systems are already beyond the pilot stage with agentic AI. They’ve tested use cases, proven the technology can work, and are now trying to scale it across more workflows, teams, and care settings. That shift is happening quickly. Hyro’s 2026 Healthcare AI Agent Benchmark Report found that 94% of current users consider AI agents critical to their 2026 operations. But the processes around those deployments are still catching up: only 59% use standardized frameworks to measure performance, while 40% still rely on informal approaches. That’s where a different set of problems starts to surface: governance teams have to coordinate more stakeholders, leaders have to build trust workflow by workflow, and operational teams have to standardize processes before AI agents can scale. At a recent CHIME Innovation Summit roundtable, digital health leaders from health systems already implementing agentic AI compared notes on what happens after the pilot. Across very different organizations, the same issues kept surfacing: overlapping governance, uneven trust, and workflows that were never standardized enough to scale. In complex care environments, health systems may need to coordinate not only their own agentic AI policies but those of partner organizations and technology vendors. In other words, the challenge of scaling agentic AI is no longer just technical. It depends on whether the organization can align governance, build trust, and standardize the workflows AI agents are expected to run. If you’re trying to scale agentic AI beyond isolated pilots, the full CHIME and Hyro white paper, Orchestrating the Agentic AI Experience: Scaling Governance, Trust, and Organizational Readiness goes deeper into what has to change inside the organization before agentic AI can scale safely and consistently. For a quick read, here are the biggest lessons shared by health system leaders already scaling agentic AI — the governance, trust, and workflow challenges they’re facing along the way. Face the governance sprawl head on If scaling agentic AI in your health system feels slower than the pilot did, governance may be the reason. The issue is rarely that there’s no oversight. More often, there’s too much of it spread across too many groups. AI governance, IT governance, digital strategy, clinical leadership, legal, compliance, and security may all have a role, but when ownership is unclear, the same questions get reviewed multiple times and no one knows which decision is final. Taylor Hamilton , Chief Digital Officer at Ballad Health , described exactly that kind of environment: separate AI governance, IT governance, and digital strategy and transformation committees, each with its own policies, charters, and roadmaps. The result is not necessarily stronger oversight. It can be duplicated work, overlapping authority, and slower decisions. Kayce Degenhardt, VP of IT Clinical Applications at Inova Health , argued for a more unified approach. Governance should connect strategy, technology, operations, and clinical care instead of treating agentic AI as a separate layer that needs its own process for every decision. She also warned that over-engineering governance can make agentic AI feel more intimidating to the teams expected to use it. For leaders trying to scale beyond a few isolated workflows, that distinction matters. The goal is not to add another committee. It’s to make clear who owns the decision, which stakeholders need to be involved, and what has to be true for an AI agent to move from one workflow to the next. That is the difference between governance that enables scale and governance that becomes the next agentic AI bottleneck . Earn trust in small workflows first Getting an AI agent approved is one thing. Getting clinicians, staff, and operational leaders comfortable enough to expand what it can do is another. That becomes especially important once agentic AI moves beyond answering questions and starts taking action. The tolerance for mistakes drops quickly when an agent is scheduling appointments, changing patient information, or handling workflows that staff are used to controlling themselves. Andy Crowder , SVP and Chief Digital and AI Officer at Advocate Health , pointed to that imbalance directly. Healthcare teams are accustomed to a certain level of human error, but they often hold technology to a much higher standard. As Crowder put it, “trust is not linear.” One successful deployment doesn’t guarantee confidence in the next use case, and a visible failure can undo progress quickly. That’s why the first workflows matter so much. Israel Krush , Hyro’s CEO and Co-Founder, recommended starting with high-volume, high-value, low-risk use cases where the decision logic is clear and the consequences of an error are limited. Screening mammograms were one example discussed at the roundtable: the workflow can deliver meaningful operational value while giving staff a chance to see the AI agents perform consistently before expanding into more complex territory. Start with the budget date, not the vendor shortlist 02. Mapping your evaluation to your fiscal calendar 03. The dual track: formal budget cycle vs. discretionary funding 04. The conversation to start today Share this post Key takeaways The best time to plan an agentic AI investment is before your budget opens, not after. Work backward from your budget date to determine when evaluation, procurement, legal review, and internal approvals need to begin. Missing the formal budget window doesn’t always mean waiting another year, but it does mean exploring a different funding path. If you’re evaluating agentic AI for patient access, the operational need is probably already clear. The next challenge is making sure the evaluation, procurement, and budgeting timelines all line up. Before you schedule another demo, find out when your budget opens. Then ask one more question: when does finance need the business case? Those two dates determine when your evaluation really needs to begin. This is where many promising initiatives lose a year. The team begins evaluating solutions, narrows the field, and only then asks when the budget request is due. By that point, legal may still be reviewing terms, procurement may not have begun, and finance may already be finalizing next year’s priorities. The problem wasn’t a lack of budget. The project wasn’t ready when funding decisions were made. One way to avoid that is by treating the budget date as the fixed point and planning backward from there. Once you know what must be ready, and by when, the evaluation timeline becomes much easier to manage. Start with the budget date, not the vendor shortlist Every health system has a budget calendar. The difference is whether you build your evaluation around it or discover its importance too late. According to the Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA), fiscal year-end dates vary across hospitals , with government-sponsored organizations commonly operating on different schedules than private health systems. Some health systems plan around the calendar year. Others, particularly state- and government-affiliated organizations, follow different fiscal calendars and frequently begin their fiscal year on October 1st, mirroring the federal government’s October 1–September 30 fiscal calendar . Whatever your organization’s cycle, it should define your evaluation timeline from the very beginning, not after you’ve narrowed the vendor list or started procurement. That’s where many teams get into trouble. The evaluation starts with vendor demos. Requirements are gathered, stakeholders compare solutions, and technical discussions begin. Only later does someone ask finance when next year’s budget submissions are due. Suddenly, every remaining step: security review, legal, procurement, executive approvals, and the business case is racing against a deadline that has been on the calendar all along. Teams that consistently secure funding approach the process differently. They start by asking when the funding decision will be made , then build every milestone backward from that date. If your organization follows a calendar-year budgeting process, we break down why many initiatives need to be scoped, justified, and submitted months before the new fiscal year begins . The mechanics differ between health systems, but the principle is the same: the budget calendar is fixed, and your evaluation timeline needs to fit around it, not the other way around. Mapping your evaluation to your fiscal calendar Once you know your budget date, you can start planning backwards. The goal isn’t to create a perfect project plan. It’s to make sure every critical milestone is completed before funding decisions are made. That starts with understanding how long each step typically takes inside your own organization. Ask yourself: When does finance need a completed business case? How long does procurement usually take? How much time should you allow for legal and information security reviews? Will architecture or governance committees need to approve the solution? Do you need operational results from a pilot before requesting funding? The answers will be different at every health system, which is exactly why this exercise matters. Too many evaluation timelines assume the only clock that matters is implementation. In reality, implementation doesn’t begin until every internal approval has already happened. Fortunately, proving value doesn’t always require a lengthy pilot. Tampa General Hospital deployed Hyro’s AI agents in just 68 days , demonstrating that organizations can generate meaningful operational evidence within a relatively short period. If your budget opens in a few months, that kind of deployment timeline may be enough to build the financial case finance expects before funding decisions are finalized. At the same time, don’t wait until procurement is complete to begin modeling the business case. You already know your call volume, staffing levels, and average handle time. Those operational inputs are enough to estimate potential financial impact early in the evaluation process. Hyro’s ROAI Calculator can help translate those assumptions into a financial model that is ready well before finance asks for it. The important question isn’t Can we deploy quickly? It’s: Can we complete evaluation, approvals, and the business case before our funding window closes? Good conversations can now be automated conversations – which means satisfied patients, better operational efficiencies and maximized returns. We call that HY-ROI. Our Mission How we got here... A (very) surface-level history of agentic AI 1966 Eliza, The first chatbot, ever. Created by Joseph Weizenbaum to simulate a psychotherapist, using simple pattern matching and substitution methodology. Worked by pairing words that patients entered into a computer with a list of pre-scripted responses. 1995 A.L.I.C.E Artificial Linguistic Internet Computer Entity (A.L.I.C.E) is a chatbot that used heuristic pattern matching to have conversations. Invented by Richard Wallace in 1995, it relied on an XML schema known as artificial intelligence markup language (AIML), which specifies conversation rules. The program simulates chatting with a real person over the Internet – in this case, Alice, a young woman who can divulge personal details and answer easy questions. 2001 Smarterchild 90’s kids can’t forget SmarterChild. At one point, it amassed 10 million users and was getting a billion messages a day. This temperamental chatbot was baked into AOL Instant Messenger (AIM) and MSN Messenger with the power to carry out fun conversations, with some additional data access to popular services at the time, like the weather and Moviefone. It’s widely considered a successful show of “conversational computing”. 2010-2014 Digital Assistants With the explosion of the iPhone came Siri for Apple iOS in 2010–an intelligent assistant and navigator that uses a natural language interface built on machine learning. Google followed suit with Google Assistant, originally launched in 2012 under a different name. Then came Cortana and Alexa in 2014. All of these digital assistants brought interactive voice into the mix, helping users send emails and texts, play music, place calls and find files, locations, and general information. 2018-2026 Large Language Models We’ll get to ChatGPT in a second. Large language models – neural networks with tons (billions) of parameters, trained on large quantities of text – came about in 2018. BERT was first on scene with 340 million parameters. But OpenAI wasn’t far behind, and shocked the world with GPT-3 in 2020, an LLM that boasted 175 billion parameters. After some fine-tuning, a variant called GPT-3.5 was made available to the public in 2022 in the form of a web interface. You guessed it. ChatGPT, the fastest growing app in history, generates human-like text and can carry out a variety of tasks, including writing scripts and translating books.
